# PT CP Forward Credits Integration

```

---

## 🔗 Related Projects

**Parent Project:** [[PT CP Carbon Plant IoM]]

**Related:**
- [[PT UK CP Reporting 202508]] - Related reporting project
- [[PT UG Exchange Bidding Upgrade]] - Related exchange work

**Organizations:**
- [[UG World]] - Client organization
- [[Carbon Plant]] - Platform

**Origin:** [[Meeting 20251022 Yanis Forward Credits]] - Forward credits gap discovered during approval workflow discussion

---

## 👥 Team

- **Product Lead:** [[Yanis Hammick]]
- **Developer:** [[Shailendra]]
- **PM:** Ignatius (you)
- **Financial Oversight:** [[Toshko Botev]]
- **Testing:** Sarah Niki Yanis

---

## ✅ Tasks

### Phase 1: Research & Design (Week 1-2)

**Research:**
- [ ] Research PURO registry API - forward credits capabilities [[Yanis Hammick]] [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Research how Patch platform handles forward credits [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Document industry standards for forward credit workflows [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Create competitive analysis document (PURO vs Patch vs others) [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Identify PURO API limitations and constraints [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Determine registry visibility rules (what shows when) [[Yanis Hammick]] [[Shailendra]]

**Design:**
- [ ] Design forward credit status tracking (states: allocated → pending → verified → live) [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Design buyer/seller visibility rules for forward credits [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Design approval workflow (verifier role for forward credits) [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Map notification triggers for forward credit state changes [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Create workflow diagrams (buyer flow, seller flow, verifier flow) [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Document edge cases and error handling [[Yanis Hammick]] [[Shailendra]]

**Documentation:**
- [ ] Write technical specification document [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Write user stories for forward credit buyers [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Write user stories for forward credit sellers [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Write user stories for forward credit verifiers [[Yanis Hammick]]

### Phase 2: Technical Architecture (Week 3)

**Backend Design:**
- [ ] Design database schema for forward credits [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Design API endpoints (create, update, verify forward credits) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Design PURO registry integration points [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Plan migration strategy for existing database [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Document error handling and edge cases [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Design forward credit state machine [[Shailendra]]

**Frontend Design:**
- [ ] Design UI mockups for forward credit displays [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Design approval flow screens [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Design forward credit transaction history [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Create component specifications [[Shailendra]]

### Phase 3: Development (Week 4-6)

**Backend Development:**
- [ ] Implement forward credit database models [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Build forward credit CRUD APIs [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Integrate PURO registry sync (if applicable) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Implement forward credit approval workflow [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Add forward credit notifications (email) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Extend sequential processing for forward credits [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Write unit tests [[Shailendra]]

**Frontend Development:**
- [ ] Build forward credit listing components [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Build forward credit detail views [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Build approval workflow UI [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Build forward credit notifications UI [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Update buyer/seller dashboards for forward credits [[Shailendra]]

**Integration:**
- [ ] Test PURO registry connection [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Test forward credit → verified credit transition [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Test notification delivery (email) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Test sequential processing of parallel requests [[Shailendra]]

### Phase 4: Testing & Launch (Week 7-8)

**Testing:**
- [ ] Unit testing (backend) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Integration testing (PURO API) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] E2E testing (full buyer/seller/verifier flows) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] UAT with Sarah and test users [[Yanis Hammick]] [[Sarah]]
- [ ] Performance testing (parallel request handling) [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Test edge cases and error scenarios [[Shailendra]]

**Launch:**
- [ ] Deploy to staging [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Final UAT approval [[Yanis Hammick]] [[Sarah]]
- [ ] Deploy to production [[Shailendra]]
- [ ] Monitor for issues (first 48 hours) [[Shailendra]] [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Document learnings [[Yanis Hammick]]
- [ ] Update user documentation [[Yanis Hammick]]

---

## 🧾 Project Description

**Problem Identified:** Current Carbon Plant platform only handles verified/live carbon credits. There is no workflow for forward credits (pre-verified credits that will be verified in the future).

**Challenge:**
- How should forward credits appear on registries before verification?
- What is the industry standard for forward credit movement?
- How do competitors (PURO, Patch) handle this?

**Solution:** Design and implement a forward credits workflow that:
- Tracks forward credits separately from verified credits
- Integrates with PURO registry appropriately
- Provides buyer/seller visibility at appropriate stages
- Maintains sequential processing of parallel requests
- Extends existing approval workflow (verifier role)

**Origin:** Meeting with [[Yanis Hammick]] on 2025-10-22 identified this gap during discussion of approval workflows.

**Project Info:**
- **Created:** 2025-10-22
- **Deadline:** [8 weeks from start - ~2025-12-15]

# 2025-10-29 Planning 


---

### **Public Sector AI & ESG Diploma: Course Blueprint (Teachable Format)**

**Total Course Duration:** 30 Hours  
**Format:** Fully asynchronous, text-based lessons with integrated practical exercises.

---

### **Section 1 — Setting the Stage: AI, Governance, and the Sustainable Future of Public Service**

- **Lesson: Welcome and Course Overview**  
    (This text introduces the 30-hour, text-based diploma. It explains the asynchronous format, the structure of the 7 sections, and emphasizes that the practical exercise in each section is a mandatory building block for the final Capstone Project, creating a single, integrated learning journey.)
    
- **Lesson: The Public Sector Mandate: ESG, AI, and Public Trust**  
    (This lesson reframes the "intersection" for government. It explains that public administrations face a dual mandate: achieving sustainability goals (like the SDGs) and leveraging technological innovation. It argues that public trust, the cornerstone of governance, now depends on mastering both.)
    
- **Lesson: ESG as a Framework for Public Administration Excellence**  
    (This lesson moves beyond the corporate view of ESG. It frames Environmental (resource management, climate resilience), Social (equitable service delivery, citizen well-being), and Governance (transparency, accountability, ethical integrity) as core pillars of effective and sustainable public administration.)
    
- **Lesson: AI as an Enabler of Modern Governance**  
    (This text introduces AI not as a disruptor, but as a fundamental enabler for the public sector. It explains that AI provides the tools to move from reactive to proactive service delivery, from estimation to data-driven policy, and from inefficiency to responsible stewardship of public funds.)
    
- **Practical Application 1: The AI Readiness & ESG Opportunity Memo**  
    (This is the first building block for the Capstone. Students will write a one-page memo identifying a key ESG challenge in their agency and proposing one AI technology from the module that could address it. This grounds the course in their immediate reality.)
    

---

### **Section 2 — AI Applications in Public Service & Sustainable Governance**

- **Lesson: Core AI Technologies for Government**  
    (This lesson provides a non-technical overview of the key AI technologies. It defines Machine Learning, NLP, Computer Vision, and Generative AI, using a specific public sector example for each, such as using NLP to analyze public comments on policy drafts.)
    
- **Lesson: AI for Environmental Stewardship (The 'E' of ESG)**  
    (This text focuses on environmental applications. It will cover use cases like AI-powered climate models for municipal planning, predictive maintenance for public water infrastructure, and computer vision for monitoring illegal deforestation or waste dumping.)
    
- **Lesson: AI for Social Equity & Citizen Services (The 'S' of ESG)**  
    (This lesson focuses on social impact. It will detail applications such as using AI to optimize public transport routes for underserved communities, identifying at-risk populations for social support programs, and creating accessible digital services for citizens with disabilities.)
    
- **Lesson: AI for Enhanced Governance and Compliance (The 'G' of ESG)**  
    (This text covers governance applications. It will explain how AI can be used for fraud and anomaly detection in public procurement, automating regulatory compliance checks, and enhancing transparency through intelligent open data portals.)
    
- **Practical Application 2: The Solution Deep Dive**  
    (Building on the previous memo, students will select their chosen ESG problem and AI solution. They will write a short paper detailing the specific AI model, the data it would need, the key stakeholders, and the expected outcome in terms of public value.)
    

---

### **Section 3 — From Strategy to Reality: Implementing AI in Government**

- **Lesson: Data Readiness & Governance: The Foundation of AI**  
    (This lesson explains that AI implementation is impossible without a solid data foundation. It covers the principles of public sector data governance, data quality, breaking down departmental silos, and ensuring data privacy and security.)
    
- **Lesson: Defining Success Metrics for Public Sector AI**  
    (This text teaches students how to evaluate AI projects beyond simple financial ROI. It will introduce metrics related to improved service delivery times, increased citizen satisfaction, enhanced equity outcomes, and resource efficiency gains.)
    
- **Lesson: Procurement, Vendor Management & Public-Private Partnerships**  
    (This is a highly practical lesson on the unique challenges of buying AI solutions for government. It covers how to write effective procurement requirements, evaluate vendor claims, manage contracts, and structure successful partnerships with the private sector.)
    
- **Practical Application 3: The Risk & Mitigation Register**  
    (Students will create a risk register for their proposed project. They will identify at least five potential risks (e.g., algorithmic bias, data privacy breach, vendor lock-in, low public adoption) and propose a specific mitigation strategy for each.)
    

---

### **Section 4 — Leadership & Change Management in the AI-Driven Public Sector**

- **Lesson: Building a Culture of Data-Driven Innovation**  
    (This text focuses on the human element. It explains the leadership actions required to foster a culture where civil servants are encouraged to experiment, use data in their daily work, and see AI as a supportive tool rather than a threat.)
    
- **Lesson: Communicating AI Initiatives to the Public and Stakeholders**  
    (This lesson provides a framework for public communication. It covers how to explain complex AI projects in simple terms, build public trust through transparency, and effectively engage with diverse stakeholders, from citizens to oversight bodies.)
    
- **Lesson: Leading Change: A Framework for AI Adoption**  
    (This text provides a formal change management model (e.g., Kotter's 8-Step Process) adapted for a public sector context. It gives leaders a structured way to guide their teams and organization through the process of adopting new AI-driven processes.)
    
- **Practical Application 4: The Stakeholder & Communications Plan**  
    (Students will develop a simple stakeholder map for their project, identifying key groups (e.g., citizens, senior leadership, IT department, union representatives). They will then draft a key message for each group explaining the project's benefits and addressing their likely concerns.)
    

---

### **Section 5 — Capstone Project: Assembling Your AI Initiative Proposal**

- **Lesson: Project Guidelines and Final Framework**  
    (This lesson provides the formal structure and requirements for the Capstone Project. It explains that the project is a comprehensive "AI Initiative Proposal" that consolidates and refines the work from the previous four practical applications.)
    
- **Lesson: Peer Feedback and Proposal Refinement**  
    (This text explains the process for a structured peer-feedback exercise. Students will be paired to review each other's draft proposals using a provided rubric, offering constructive criticism to strengthen the final submission.)
    
- **Lesson: Final Submission and Evaluation Criteria**  
    (This provides the final checklist for the Capstone submission. It clearly outlines the grading rubric, which will be based on the project's feasibility, strategic alignment with ESG principles, clarity, and the robustness of the risk and stakeholder analysis.)
    

---

### **Section 6 — Resources and Support**

- **Lesson: Additional Reading and Public Sector AI Toolkits**  
    (This text provides a curated list of high-quality external resources, such as reports from the OECD, World Bank, and national AI strategy documents, as well as links to open-source public sector AI toolkits.)
    
- **Lesson: The Role of the AI Coach**  
    (This lesson explains how students can use the AI Coach for continuous support throughout the course, providing examples of effective prompts for brainstorming ideas, refining their writing, and getting feedback on their projects.)
    
- **Lesson: Community Forums for Peer Collaboration**  
    (This text outlines the guidelines for using the community forums, encouraging students to ask questions, share resources, and collaborate with their peers from across the public sector.)
    
- **Lesson: Course Evaluation and Next Steps**  
    (The final lesson provides the course evaluation form and suggests next steps for continuing their learning journey in AI and public administration, such as joining professional networks or exploring further certifications.)

# 💰 Business Model & Billing Strategy

**Updated:** 2025-10-22 - [[Meeting 20251022]] with [[Michael Cosgrave]]

## Two Revenue Models

### 1. SaaS Model (Primary Strategy)

**First Client Implementation:**
- **Implementation Fee:** $20,000 per site
- **Monthly License:** $1,500 per month per site/seat
- **Scalable:** Each additional site = new implementation + recurring revenue

**Example Revenue:**
- 50 data centers × $20K implementation = $1M upfront
- 50 sites × $1.5K/month = $75K MRR ($900K ARR)
- **Total Year 1:** $1.9M revenue

### 2. Perpetual License Model (Exit/Large Client Strategy)

**For major clients controlling significant market share:**

**Pricing Structure:**
- Calculate 3-year SaaS equivalent revenue
- Add premium for opportunity cost (% of market they control)
- Example: Client controls 30% of 2,500 data centers (750 sites)
  - 3-year SaaS value: 750 × $20K + (750 × $1.5K × 36 months) = $55.5M
  - Plus market control premium
  - Negotiated perpetual license price

**License Controls:**
- Software includes site limits (licensed for X sites)
- System blocks additional site creation beyond license
- Upsell for additional capacity

**Target Buyers:**
- Major operators (CP, E) controlling 30%+ market share
- Companies wanting to own vs rent
- Strategic acquisitions

---

## Strategic Purpose: "Enabling Technology"

**DOME = Door Opener, Not Just Revenue**

### Primary Value
- Gets GlenArt into conversations with major clients
- Opens doors that wouldn't otherwise exist
- Builds relationships at institutional level
- Creates 10-20-30 year business opportunities

### Michael's Approach
- Wants **2 years of exposure** before considering full sale
- Focus: leverage DOME for broader GlenArt business development
- Not optimizing for quick exit - building long-term relationships
- Even 50 data centers is "pretty lucrative"

### Revenue as Validation
- Product will pay for itself quickly (low investment, high margins)
- Real value = access to tier-1 clients and decision makers
- Similar to [[PT 202506 Yentra USA VET EVOLVE|EVOLVE]] - enabling tech for bigger opportunities

### 1️⃣ User Roles & Account Basics (Tasks 1.1 - 1.8)

#### Task 1.1: Implement Two-Tier User Account System
**Description**: Create separate account types for Candidate and Employer with role-based access control

**Technical Specs**:
- Database schema with `user_type` enum: ['candidate', 'employer', 'admin']
- Role-based middleware for route protection
- Separate registration flows for each role

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Users can register as either Candidate or Employer
- [ ] Employers can only view their own job applications
- [ ] Role is immutable after account creation

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django User model with custom AbstractUser
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

#### Task 1.2: Email + Password Authentication
**Description**: Implement secure email/password authentication system

**Technical Specs**:
- Email validation (RFC 5322 compliant)
- Password requirements: min 12 chars, uppercase, lowercase, number, special char
- Rate limiting on login attempts (5 attempts per 15 min)

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Users register with valid email format
- [ ] Passwords meet security requirements
- [ ] Failed login attempts are rate-limited

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django authentication system
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

#### Task 1.3: Employer-Only Applicant Access
**Description**: Ensure employers can only access applicants for their own job postings

**Technical Specs**:
- Database queries filtered by `employer_id`
- Authorization checks before displaying applicant data
- Audit log for applicant profile views

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Employers see only their applicants
- [ ] Direct URL access to other applicants is blocked
- [ ] All applicant views are logged

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django ORM query filtering
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

#### Task 1.5: HTTPS Enforcement
**Description**: Enforce HTTPS for all connections

**Technical Specs**:
- HTTPS redirect middleware (HTTP → HTTPS 301)
- HSTS header: `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains`

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] All HTTP requests redirect to HTTPS
- [ ] HSTS header present on all responses
- [ ] Cookies have secure flags set

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT setting
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

**Description**: Implement secure password hashing

**Technical Specs**:
- Use argon2id algorithm (preferred) or bcrypt

- Password rehashing on login if algorithm upgraded

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Passwords never stored in plaintext
- [ ] Hash algorithm is argon2id or bcrypt
- [ ] Old hashes auto-upgraded on user login

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django PASSWORD_HASHERS setting
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

- System prompts confirmation
- Deletion logged with `deleted_by: 'admin'`

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Admin can delete by email
- [ ] Requires admin authentication
- [ ] Logs admin user ID

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django admin action
**Priority**: P1 (High)

---

#### Task 3.6: Employer Account Deletion Rules
**Description**: Special handling for employer deletions

**Technical Specs**:
- Check for active job postings
- If active jobs exist:
  - Show warning: "Close or expire all jobs first"
  - Block deletion until jobs closed
- If no active jobs: proceed with deletion

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Deletion blocked if active jobs exist
- [ ] Warning message displayed
- [ ] Deletion succeeds when no active jobs

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Pre-deletion validation
**Priority**: P1 (High)

### 4️⃣ Data Retention Schedule (9 Tasks)

#### Task 4.1: Active Candidate Account Retention
**Description**: Retain active candidate accounts indefinitely while in use

**Technical Specs**:
- Track `last_login` timestamp
- Account considered "active" if logged in within 36 months
- No automated deletion while active

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] `last_login` updated on each login
- [ ] Active accounts never auto-deleted

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django last_login field
**Priority**: P1 (High)

---

#### Task 4.2: Inactive Candidate Account Auto-Deletion
**Description**: Delete candidate accounts after 36 months of inactivity

**Technical Specs**:
- Cron job runs monthly: `0 2 1 * *` (1st of month, 2am)
- Query: `last_login < NOW() - INTERVAL '36 months'`
- Send warning email 30 days before deletion
- Delete account if still inactive

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Warning email sent 30 days before
- [ ] Deletion occurs at 36 months
- [ ] Cron job logs activity

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django management command + cron
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

---

#### Task 4.3: Job Application Retention (18 Months After Job Closure)
**Description**: Delete applications 18 months after associated job closes

**Technical Specs**:
- Track `job_closed_at` timestamp on job postings
- Cron job: Delete applications where `job_closed_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '18 months'`
- Delete: CV files, application data, messages

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Applications deleted 18 months post-closure
- [ ] CV files removed from storage
- [ ] Deletion logged

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django management command
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

---

#### Task 4.4: Job Posting Retention (24 Months After Expiry)
**Description**: Delete job postings 24 months after expiry

**Technical Specs**:
- Track `expired_at` timestamp
- Cron job: Delete postings where `expired_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '24 months'`
- Preserve anonymised analytics data

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Job postings deleted after 24 months
- [ ] Analytics export runs before deletion
- [ ] Deletion logged

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Django management command
**Priority**: P0 (Critical)

---

#### Task 4.5: Employer Account Retention (7 Years After Closure)
**Description**: Retain employer accounts for 7 years for legal/tax purposes

**Technical Specs**:
- Track `account_closed_at` timestamp
- Employer accounts marked as "closed" (not deleted immediately)
- Cron job: Delete after 7 years

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Employer accounts retained 7 years
- [ ] Account status: active/closed/deleted
- [ ] Financial data retained with account

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django soft-delete pattern
**Priority**: P1 (High)

---

#### Task 4.6: Financial Records Retention (7 Years)
**Description**: Retain invoices, payments, tax records for 7 years

**Technical Specs**:
- Separate table: `financial_records`
- Linked to employer account
- Never auto-deleted until 7-year mark

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Financial records separate from user data
- [ ] Retained regardless of account deletion
- [ ] Deleted only after 7 years

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Separate financial table
**Priority**: P1 (High)

---

#### Task 4.7: Usage Logs Retention (24 Months)
**Description**: Delete usage logs after 24 months, then aggregate

**Technical Specs**:
- Logs include: logins, page views, searches
- Cron job: Archive to aggregated metrics, then delete
- Aggregated data: daily counts (no user IDs)

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Logs deleted after 24 months
- [ ] Aggregated metrics preserved
- [ ] No personal data in aggregates

**Complexity**: Medium
**References**: Log aggregation script
**Priority**: P2 (Medium)

---

#### Task 4.8: Support Ticket Retention (12 Months After Resolution)
**Description**: Delete support messages 12 months after ticket closed

**Technical Specs**:
- Track `resolved_at` timestamp
- Cron job: Delete tickets where `resolved_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '12 months'`

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Tickets deleted 12 months post-resolution
- [ ] Summary stats preserved (anonymised)

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Django management command
**Priority**: P2 (Medium)

---

#### Task 4.9: Marketing Consent Log Retention (Until Withdrawal + 24 Months)
**Description**: Retain marketing consent logs for evidence

**Technical Specs**:
- Table: `marketing_consent`
  - `user_id`, `consented_at`, `withdrawn_at`, `proof_kept_until`
- Calculate: `proof_kept_until = withdrawn_at + 24 months`
- Cron job: Delete when `NOW() > proof_kept_until`

**Acceptance Criteria**:
- [ ] Consent logs retained 24 months after withdrawal
- [ ] Logs deleted automatically after period

**Complexity**: Low
**References**: Separate consent table
**Priority**: P2 (Medium)

# Obsidian Knowledge Management Skill

## Core Purpose

Manage Ignatius's Obsidian Personal vault with focus on:
1. **People & Relationships** - Track who you work with and relationship closeness/importance
2. **Project Connections** - Map people to active projects and analyze collaboration patterns
3. **Knowledge Graph Maintenance** - Keep vault structure clean and well-linked
4. **List Management** - Update people lists, project summaries, and relationship tracking

## Vault Structure

**Base Path:** `/Users/irautenbach/Documents/Obsidian/Personal/`

**Key Directories:**
- `3 Efforts/ON/` - Active projects (PT/OPT files)
- `3 Efforts/Ongoing/` - Ongoing projects
- `3 Efforts Notes/` - Project support notes
- `Atlas Dots/` - Individual atomic notes (people, concepts, tools)
- `Atlas Dots/Lists/` - Curated lists (People - Active Projects, etc.)
- `Atlas Maps/` - Map of Contents (MOCs) organizing topics
- `Companies/` - Company notes
- `Diary/` - Daily entries
- `0 INBOX/` - Unsorted incoming notes

## Relationship Closeness Framework

Use this framework to categorize people by their closeness/importance to Ignatius's life and work:

### Tier 1: Core (Pivotal to Life & Work)
**Characteristics:**
- Daily/weekly interaction
- Critical to multiple major projects
- Deep trust and long-term relationship
- Significant impact on business/personal outcomes
- Would significantly affect trajectory if relationship ended

**Examples from current projects:**
- Family (Yvette, children)
- Kirsty Chadwick (TTRO - multiple strategic opportunities)
- Ron Dahlgren (Connected IQ - technical foundation partner)
- Michael Cosgrave (Glenart - strategic business partner)

### Tier 2: Strategic Partners (High Importance)
**Characteristics:**
- Regular interaction (weekly/bi-weekly)
- Key to 1-2 major projects
- Proven track record of delivery
- Strategic value to business growth
- Strong professional relationship

**Examples from current projects:**
- Yanis Hammick (Carbon Plant - product lead)
- David Halley (Gfinity/Connected IQ - recurring partner)
- Adam Shore (Liverpool University - institutional partnership)
- Miles Ashworth (IoM client - ongoing projects)

### Tier 3: Active Collaborators (Regular Contact)
**Characteristics:**
- Project-based interaction
- Specific expertise/role in current work
- Reliable delivery on defined scope
- Professional relationship established
- May become strategic over time

**Examples from current projects:**
- Shailendra (Developer - Carbon Plant)
- Steward Collier (Technical lead - DOME)
- Jim Finnegan (PocketBox - opportunity development)
- Keith Zammit (Malta - networking/opportunities)

### Tier 4: Occasional/Emerging (New or Infrequent)
**Characteristics:**
- Early-stage relationship
- Infrequent interaction
- Potential for growth
- Single project or exploratory
- Networking/opportunity contacts

**Examples from current projects:**
- Judy (Mazars - new opportunity)
- Emirati lady (Dubai Airports - new contact)
- Stefan (FieldStream.ai - Malta opportunity)
- Barney Bryson (InvestNI - meeting scheduled)

### Tier 5: Passive (Past or Minimal Contact)
**Characteristics:**
- No current active projects
- Historical relationship
- Occasional check-ins
- May re-activate in future
- Archived project contacts

## Primary Workflows

### 1. Update People Lists from Active Projects

**When to use:** After project status updates, new project starts, or relationship changes

**Process:**
1. Scan `/3 Efforts/ON/` and `/3 Efforts/Ongoing/` for PT/OPT files
2. Extract people mentioned in:
   - Team sections
   - Contact lists
   - References
   - Meeting notes
3. Identify their roles and project involvement
4. Categorize by relationship tier (1-5)
5. Update `Atlas Dots/Lists/People - Active Projects.md`
6. Flag any changes in relationship importance

**Output:** Updated people list with tier classifications

### 2. Analyze Relationship Patterns

**When to use:** Weekly/monthly reviews, strategic planning, or when asked "who am I working with most?"

**Process:**
1. Count project appearances per person
2. Analyze interaction frequency from Diary entries
3. Map people to project outcomes (health, status)
4. Identify:
   - Multi-project collaborators (strategic partners)
   - Single-point dependencies (risk)
   - Emerging relationships (potential strategic)
   - Declining relationships (past collaborators)
5. Suggest tier adjustments based on data

**Output:** Relationship analysis with recommendations

### 3. Create/Update Person Notes

**When to use:** New contact introduced, relationship tier changes, or person becomes pivotal

**Person Note Template Location:** Check for templates in vault
**Person Note Storage:** `Atlas Dots/` directory (individual atomic notes)

**Required Fields:**
```yaml
---
tags:
  - person
  - tier/[1-5]
  - [industry tags]
relationship_tier: [1-5]
first_met: YYYY-MM-DD
last_contact: YYYY-MM-DD
primary_projects: [list]
expertise: [list]
organization: [[Company Name]]
---

# [Person Name]

## Relationship Context
- **Tier:** [1-5] - [Core/Strategic/Active/Occasional/Passive]
- **Primary Connection:** [How you met/primary context]
- **Key Projects:** [[Project 1]], [[Project 2]]
- **Organization:** [[Company/Institution]]

## Expertise & Value
- [What they bring to collaborations]
- [Key skills/knowledge]
- [Strategic value]

## Active Projects
- [[PT/OPT Project Name]] - [Role]

## Communication Notes
- Preferred contact: [email/WhatsApp/etc]
- Response time: [typical]
- Communication style: [notes]

## History
[Reverse chronological notes on key interactions]
```

### 4. Map People to Projects

**When to use:** Understanding team structures, identifying collaboration patterns, planning resource allocation

**Process:**
1. Read all active project files
2. Create relationship map:
   - Person → Projects (one-to-many)
   - Project → People (one-to-many)
   - Person → Person (through shared projects)
3. Identify collaboration clusters
4. Highlight cross-project teams
5. Flag single-person dependencies

**Output:** Network analysis showing collaboration patterns

### 5. Relationship Health Monitoring

**When to use:** Weekly reviews, when relationships feel strained, or proactively

**Signals to track:**
- Last contact date vs. typical frequency
- Project health where they're involved
- Response time changes
- Scope/deliverable issues
- Communication tone shifts

**Actions:**
- Flag relationships needing attention
- Suggest check-in contacts
- Identify potential conflicts
- Recommend relationship maintenance

## Obsidian-Specific Conventions

### Linking Standards
- **People:** `[[Person Name]]` - links to person note in Atlas Dots
- **Projects:** `[[PT/OPT Project Name]]` - links to project file in 3 Efforts
- **Companies:** `[[Company Name]]` - links to company note
- **Locations:** `[[City, Country]]` - links to location notes
- **Concepts:** `[[Concept Name]]` - links to concept notes

### Tag Structure
```yaml
person tags:
  - person
  - tier/1, tier/2, tier/3, tier/4, tier/5
  - industry/tech, industry/education, industry/finance, etc.
  - role/developer, role/client, role/partner, etc.
  - geo/uk, geo/usa, geo/malta, geo/dubai, etc.
```

### Metadata Standards
- Use YAML frontmatter for all structured data
- Date format: `YYYY-MM-DD`
- Modified dates: Update on significant changes only
- Status values: `active`, `passive`, `archived`

## Integration with Project Management

### Project File Analysis
When analyzing projects, extract:
- **Team sections** - Direct collaborators
- **References sections** - Related people
- **Meeting notes** - Interaction history
- **Next actions** - Who's responsible
- **Blockers** - Dependency analysis

### Diary Integration
Cross-reference Diary entries to:
- Track actual interaction frequency
- Capture relationship context
- Identify communication patterns
- Note relationship changes in real-time

### Weekly Review Support
During weekly reviews:
1. Update relationship tiers based on activity
2. Flag relationships needing attention
3. Identify new strategic relationships
4. Archive passive relationships
5. Update people lists

## Key Operations

### Operation: Full People List Refresh

**Trigger:** "Update my people list" or "Refresh active project collaborators"

**Steps:**
1. Scan `/3 Efforts/ON/*.md` and `/3 Efforts/Ongoing/*.md`
2. Extract all people mentions with roles
3. Categorize by project and relationship tier
4. Update `Atlas Dots/Lists/People - Active Projects.md`
5. Flag new people or tier changes
6. Report summary of changes

### Operation: Relationship Tier Assessment

**Trigger:** "How close am I to [person]?" or "Assess my relationship with [person]"

**Steps:**
1. Count project appearances
2. Analyze last contact date
3. Review project outcomes where involved
4. Check communication frequency in Diary
5. Assess strategic importance
6. Recommend tier classification
7. Suggest relationship actions

### Operation: Find Single-Point Dependencies

**Trigger:** "Who am I too dependent on?" or "Find relationship risks"

**Steps:**
1. Map people to critical projects
2. Identify people who are sole contact for important work
3. Flag Tier 1/2 people with single-project involvement
4. Suggest relationship diversification
5. Recommend backup relationship building

### Operation: Discover Emerging Strategic Relationships

**Trigger:** "Who's becoming more important?" or "Find emerging relationships"

**Steps:**
1. Identify Tier 3/4 people appearing in multiple projects
2. Track increasing interaction frequency
3. Analyze project health correlation
4. Flag candidates for tier promotion
5. Suggest relationship deepening actions

## Automation Opportunities

### Proactive Triggers
Monitor for:
- New person mentioned in project notes → Suggest creating person note
- Person appears in 3+ projects → Flag as potential strategic relationship
- No contact with Tier 1/2 person for >30 days → Suggest check-in
- Project with single-person dependency → Flag risk
- Tier 3 person in multiple successful projects → Suggest tier promotion

### Weekly Automation
Run automatically during weekly review:
1. Relationship tier assessment for all active collaborators
2. Identify stale relationships (no contact >60 days)
3. Flag new people needing person notes
4. Update people lists
5. Generate relationship health report

## Example Queries

**Finding people:**

# Obsidian Persons - Complete Relationship Management System

**Version:** 1.0
**Created:** 2025-11-09
**Purpose:** Comprehensive system for managing people, relationships, and collaboration patterns in Ignatius's Obsidian vault

---

## Table of Contents

1. [System Overview](#system-overview)
2. [Vault Structure](#vault-structure)
3. [Relationship Tier Framework](#relationship-tier-framework)
4. [Core Workflows](#core-workflows)
5. [Person Note Templates](#person-note-templates)
6. [Automation & Monitoring](#automation--monitoring)
7. [Obsidian Conventions](#obsidian-conventions)
8. [Advanced Operations](#advanced-operations)
9. [Integration Patterns](#integration-patterns)
10. [Success Metrics](#success-metrics)

---

## System Overview

### Philosophy

This system treats **relationships as the foundation of all work**. Projects succeed or fail based on the people involved. By tracking relationship closeness, collaboration patterns, and interaction health, we can:

- Identify strategic partners worth investing in
- Catch relationship issues before they become project blockers
- Discover emerging collaborators who deserve more attention
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections with core relationships

### Core Capabilities

1. **People List Management** - Maintain accurate, categorized lists of who you work with
2. **Relationship Tier Assessment** - Objectively evaluate closeness/importance (1-5 scale)
3. **Collaboration Analysis** - Map people to projects, find patterns, identify risks
4. **Person Note Creation** - Individual pages for key relationships with context
5. **Health Monitoring** - Track interaction frequency, flag stale relationships
6. **Strategic Planning** - Identify who to invest in, who to maintain, who to archive

---

## Vault Structure

### Base Path
```
/Users/irautenbach/Documents/Obsidian/Personal/
```

### Key Directories

**Projects & Efforts:**
```
3 Efforts/ON/           # Active projects (PT*.md, OPT*.md files)
3 Efforts/Ongoing/      # Ongoing projects
3 Efforts Notes/        # Project support notes and resources
```

**Knowledge Base:**
```
Atlas Dots/             # Atomic notes (people, concepts, tools)
Atlas Dots/Lists/       # Curated lists (People - Active Projects, etc.)
Atlas Maps/             # Maps of Content (MOCs) organizing topics
```

**Reference & History:**
```
Companies/              # Company/organization notes
Diary/                  # Daily entries (track interactions)
0 INBOX/                # Unsorted incoming notes
```

### File Naming Conventions

**Project files:**
- `PT [Project Name].md` - Personal projects
- `OPT [Opportunity Name].md` - Business opportunities

**Person files:**
- `[First Last].md` - Individual person notes (in Atlas Dots/)

**List files:**
- `People - [Category].md` - Curated people lists (in Atlas Dots/Lists/)

---

## Relationship Tier Framework

### 5-Tier System

People are categorized by their **closeness** and **importance** to your life and work. Tiers should be based on objective data, not just feelings.

---

### Tier 1: Core (Pivotal to Life & Work)

**Definition:** These people are foundational. Your work and life would be significantly different without them.

**Characteristics:**
- Daily or weekly interaction
- Critical to multiple major projects
- Deep trust and long-term relationship (typically 1+ years)
- Significant impact on business/personal trajectory
- Losing this relationship would require major adjustment
- High emotional and professional investment

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 3+ active projects
- Contact every 1-14 days
- Projects with them have high success rate
- Recurring collaboration over 12+ months
- Decision-making influence

**Maintenance:**
- Proactive contact every 1-2 weeks minimum
- Regular check-ins beyond project needs
- Invest in relationship deepening
- Priority response time
- Share strategic thinking

**Current examples:**
- **Family:** Yvette (wife), Taia, Judah, Caleb, Gabriel (children)
- **Strategic partners:** Kirsty Chadwick (TTRO - multiple opportunities), Ron Dahlgren (Connected IQ - technical foundation), Michael Cosgrave (Glenart - strategic business)

**Typical roles:**
- Life partner, immediate family
- Co-founders, business partners
- Long-term strategic collaborators
- Key advisors with proven track record

---

### Tier 2: Strategic Partners (High Importance)

**Definition:** Highly important to current success, key to 1-2 major initiatives.

**Characteristics:**
- Regular interaction (weekly to bi-weekly)
- Key to 1-2 major projects (not just supporting role)
- Proven track record of delivery
- Strategic value to business growth
- Strong professional relationship
- Would impact success if relationship ended

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1-2 active projects in key roles
- Contact every 1-4 weeks
- Reliable delivery and communication
- Projects with them generally succeed
- Mutual value exchange

**Maintenance:**
- Contact every 2-4 weeks
- Regular project check-ins
- Occasional non-project relationship building
- Good response priority
- Share relevant opportunities

**Current examples:**
- Yanis Hammick (Carbon Plant - product lead)
- David Halley (Gfinity/Connected IQ - recurring partner)
- Adam Shore (Liverpool University - institutional partnership)
- Miles Ashworth (IoM - ongoing client projects)

**Typical roles:**
- Key clients with ongoing work
- Primary contacts at strategic organizations
- Reliable technical leads
- Important institutional partners

---

### Tier 3: Active Collaborators (Regular Contact)

**Definition:** Active working relationships with specific scope and regular interaction.

**Characteristics:**
- Project-based interaction (during active phases)
- Specific expertise or defined role
- Reliable within their scope
- Professional relationship established
- Could become strategic over time
- Relationship tied to project lifecycle

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1 active project
- Contact every 1-8 weeks (project-dependent)
- Delivers on defined scope
- Professional but not deeply personal
- Clear role and boundaries

**Maintenance:**
- Contact based on project needs
- Professional communication
- Responsive to their needs
- Evaluate for tier promotion if multi-project collaboration emerges

**Current examples:**
- Shailendra (Developer - Carbon Plant)
- Steward Collier (Technical lead - DOME)
- Jim Finnegan (PocketBox - opportunity development)
- Keith Zammit (Malta - networking/opportunities)
- Toshko Botev (Financial oversight)

**Typical roles:**
- Developers on specific projects
- Subject matter experts
- Professional service providers
- Active opportunity contacts

---

### Tier 4: Occasional/Emerging (New or Infrequent)

**Definition:** Early-stage relationships or infrequent collaborators with potential.

**Characteristics:**
- New relationship (< 6 months)
- Infrequent interaction
- Exploratory or single-project
- Potential for growth unclear
- Still establishing trust and value
- Networking or opportunistic

**Data signals:**
- Recently met or minimal project involvement
- Contact every 1-3 months (or sporadic)
- Single meeting/project or exploratory discussions
- Potential value not yet proven
- Relationship still being evaluated

**Maintenance:**
- Opportunistic contact
- Responsive when they reach out
- Evaluate after 3-6 months
- Low-cost relationship investment
- Monitor for tier promotion signals

**Current examples:**
- Judy (Mazars Institute - new opportunity)
- Emirati lady (Dubai Airports - new contact)
- Stefan (FieldStream.ai - Malta opportunity)
- Barney Bryson (InvestNI - meeting scheduled)
- Brendan Kenny (Isle of Man)

**Typical roles:**
- New business contacts
- Conference/event connections
- Referral introductions
- Exploratory opportunity contacts
- Network connections

---

### Tier 5: Passive (Past or Minimal Contact)

**Definition:** Historical relationships, past collaborators, or inactive connections.

**Characteristics:**
- No current active projects
- Minimal or no interaction (3+ months)
- Completed/ended project history
- Relationship may reactivate in future
- Low current relevance
- Archived but not forgotten

**Data signals:**
- No appearance in active projects
- Last contact > 90 days
- Project completion or opportunity passed
- No active mutual value exchange
- Relationship on hold

**Maintenance:**
- Passive monitoring only
- Annual check-in (optional)
- Responsive if they reach out
- Consider archiving person note
- Re-tier if relationship reactivates

**Current examples:**
- Past project collaborators
- Declined opportunities
- Moved on to other roles
- Archived business contacts

**Typical roles:**
- Former colleagues
- Past clients
- Completed project teams
- Stale networking contacts

---

### Tier Movement Signals

**Promotion signals (move up a tier):**
- Appearing in additional projects
- Increasing interaction frequency
- Growing strategic importance
- Proven reliability and value
- Relationship deepening naturally
- Mutual investment increasing

**Demotion signals (move down a tier):**
- Decreasing interaction frequency
- Project completion/ending
- Reduced responsiveness
- Strategic importance declining
- Natural relationship drift
- One-sided effort

**Assessment cadence:**
- Tier 1-2: Review quarterly
- Tier 3: Review every 6 months
- Tier 4-5: Review annually or when reactivated

---

## Core Workflows

### Workflow 1: Update People Lists from Active Projects

**Trigger:** After project updates, new projects start, monthly review

**Process:**

```
1. SCAN PROJECT FILES
   - Read all files in /3 Efforts/ON/*.md
   - Read all files in /3 Efforts/Ongoing/*.md
   - Focus on PT* and OPT* files (project/opportunity files)

2. EXTRACT PEOPLE DATA
   For each project file, extract:
   - Team sections (## Team, ## Key Contacts, etc.)
   - People mentioned in References sections
   - Names in meeting notes
   - Contact lists
   - @mentions or [[Person Name]] links

   Capture for each person:
   - Full name
   - Role in project
   - Organization (if mentioned)
   - Project they're involved with

3. CATEGORIZE BY TIER
   For each person found, assess tier using:
   - Number of projects they appear in
   - Roles they play (lead, strategic, support)
   - Known relationship history
   - Interaction frequency (if available from Diary)

   Apply tier framework:
   - 3+ projects + key roles = Tier 1-2 candidate
   - 1-2 projects + active role = Tier 2-3
   - Single project = Tier 3-4
   - Mentioned but no active role = Tier 4-5

4. UPDATE MASTER LIST
   - Open: Atlas Dots/Lists/People - Active Projects.md
   - Organize by:
     * Family (always at top)
     * Project categories (Carbon Plant, EVOLVE, TTRO, etc.)
     * Recurring collaborators section
   - For each person, list:
     * Name with [[wiki link]]
     * Role/title
     * Projects involved
     * Organization
   - Use consistent formatting

5. FLAG CHANGES
   Compare to previous version:
   - New people added
   - People appearing in new projects

## Table of Contents

## System Overview

### Philosophy

This system treats **relationships as the foundation of all work**. Projects succeed or fail based on the people involved. By tracking relationship closeness, collaboration patterns, and interaction health, we can:

- Identify strategic partners worth investing in
- Catch relationship issues before they become project blockers
- Discover emerging collaborators who deserve more attention
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections with core relationships

### Core Capabilities

1. **People List Management** - Maintain accurate, categorized lists of who you work with
2. **Relationship Tier Assessment** - Objectively evaluate closeness/importance (1-5 scale)
3. **Collaboration Analysis** - Map people to projects, find patterns, identify risks
4. **Person Note Creation** - Individual pages for key relationships with context
5. **Health Monitoring** - Track interaction frequency, flag stale relationships
6. **Strategic Planning** - Identify who to invest in, who to maintain, who to archive

---

## Vault Structure

### Base Path
```
/Users/irautenbach/Documents/Obsidian/Personal/
```

### Key Directories

**Projects & Efforts:**
```
3 Efforts/ON/           # Active projects (PT*.md, OPT*.md files)

---

### 5-Tier System

People are categorized by their **closeness** and **importance** to your life and work. Tiers should be based on objective data, not just feelings.

---

### Tier 1: Core (Pivotal to Life & Work)

**Definition:** These people are foundational. Your work and life would be significantly different without them.

**Characteristics:**
- Daily or weekly interaction
- Critical to multiple major projects
- Deep trust and long-term relationship (typically 1+ years)
- Significant impact on business/personal trajectory
- Losing this relationship would require major adjustment
- High emotional and professional investment

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 3+ active projects
- Contact every 1-14 days
- Projects with them have high success rate
- Recurring collaboration over 12+ months
- Decision-making influence

**Maintenance:**
- Proactive contact every 1-2 weeks minimum
- Regular check-ins beyond project needs
- Invest in relationship deepening
- Priority response time
- Share strategic thinking

**Current examples:**
- **Family:** Yvette (wife), Taia, Judah, Caleb, Gabriel (children)
- **Strategic partners:** Kirsty Chadwick (TTRO - multiple opportunities), Ron Dahlgren (Connected IQ - technical foundation), Michael Cosgrave (Glenart - strategic business)

**Typical roles:**
- Life partner, immediate family
- Co-founders, business partners
- Long-term strategic collaborators
- Key advisors with proven track record

---

### Tier 2: Strategic Partners (High Importance)

**Definition:** Highly important to current success, key to 1-2 major initiatives.

**Characteristics:**
- Regular interaction (weekly to bi-weekly)
- Key to 1-2 major projects (not just supporting role)
- Proven track record of delivery
- Strategic value to business growth
- Strong professional relationship
- Would impact success if relationship ended

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1-2 active projects in key roles
- Contact every 1-4 weeks
- Reliable delivery and communication
- Projects with them generally succeed
- Mutual value exchange

**Maintenance:**
- Contact every 2-4 weeks
- Regular project check-ins
- Occasional non-project relationship building
- Good response priority
- Share relevant opportunities

**Current examples:**
- Yanis Hammick (Carbon Plant - product lead)
- David Halley (Gfinity/Connected IQ - recurring partner)
- Adam Shore (Liverpool University - institutional partnership)
- Miles Ashworth (IoM - ongoing client projects)

**Typical roles:**
- Key clients with ongoing work
- Primary contacts at strategic organizations
- Reliable technical leads
- Important institutional partners

---

### Tier 3: Active Collaborators (Regular Contact)

**Definition:** Active working relationships with specific scope and regular interaction.

**Characteristics:**
- Project-based interaction (during active phases)
- Specific expertise or defined role
- Reliable within their scope
- Professional relationship established
- Could become strategic over time
- Relationship tied to project lifecycle

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1 active project
- Contact every 1-8 weeks (project-dependent)
- Delivers on defined scope
- Professional but not deeply personal
- Clear role and boundaries

**Maintenance:**
- Contact based on project needs
- Professional communication
- Responsive to their needs
- Evaluate for tier promotion if multi-project collaboration emerges

**Current examples:**
- Shailendra (Developer - Carbon Plant)
- Steward Collier (Technical lead - DOME)
- Jim Finnegan (PocketBox - opportunity development)
- Keith Zammit (Malta - networking/opportunities)
- Toshko Botev (Financial oversight)

**Typical roles:**
- Developers on specific projects
- Subject matter experts
- Professional service providers
- Active opportunity contacts

**Definition:** Early-stage relationships or infrequent collaborators with potential.

**Characteristics:**
- New relationship (< 6 months)
- Infrequent interaction
- Exploratory or single-project
- Potential for growth unclear
- Still establishing trust and value
- Networking or opportunistic

**Data signals:**
- Recently met or minimal project involvement
- Contact every 1-3 months (or sporadic)
- Single meeting/project or exploratory discussions
- Potential value not yet proven
- Relationship still being evaluated

**Maintenance:**
- Opportunistic contact
- Responsive when they reach out
- Evaluate after 3-6 months
- Low-cost relationship investment
- Monitor for tier promotion signals

**Current examples:**
- Judy (Mazars Institute - new opportunity)
- Emirati lady (Dubai Airports - new contact)
- Stefan (FieldStream.ai - Malta opportunity)
- Barney Bryson (InvestNI - meeting scheduled)
- Brendan Kenny (Isle of Man)

**Typical roles:**
- New business contacts
- Conference/event connections
- Referral introductions
- Exploratory opportunity contacts
- Network connections

---

### Tier 5: Passive (Past or Minimal Contact)

**Definition:** Historical relationships, past collaborators, or inactive connections.

**Characteristics:**
- No current active projects
- Minimal or no interaction (3+ months)
- Completed/ended project history
- Relationship may reactivate in future
- Low current relevance
- Archived but not forgotten

**Data signals:**
- No appearance in active projects
- Last contact > 90 days
- Project completion or opportunity passed
- No active mutual value exchange
- Relationship on hold

**Maintenance:**
- Passive monitoring only
- Annual check-in (optional)
- Responsive if they reach out
- Consider archiving person note
- Re-tier if relationship reactivates

**Current examples:**
- Past project collaborators
- Declined opportunities
- Moved on to other roles
- Archived business contacts

**Typical roles:**
- Former colleagues
- Past clients
- Completed project teams
- Stale networking contacts

---

### Tier Movement Signals

**Promotion signals (move up a tier):**
- Appearing in additional projects
- Increasing interaction frequency
- Growing strategic importance
- Proven reliability and value
- Relationship deepening naturally
- Mutual investment increasing

**Demotion signals (move down a tier):**
- Decreasing interaction frequency
- Project completion/ending
- Reduced responsiveness
- Strategic importance declining
- Natural relationship drift
- One-sided effort

**Assessment cadence:**
- Tier 1-2: Review quarterly
- Tier 3: Review every 6 months
- Tier 4-5: Review annually or when reactivated

---

2. EXTRACT PEOPLE DATA

   - Full name
   - Role in project
   - Organization (if mentioned)
   - Project they're involved with

3. CATEGORIZE BY TIER
   For each person found, assess tier using:
   - Number of projects they appear in
   - Roles they play (lead, strategic, support)

   - Interaction frequency (if available from Diary)

   Apply tier framework:
   - 3+ projects + key roles = Tier 1-2 candidate
   - 1-2 projects + active role = Tier 2-3

   - Open: Atlas Dots/Lists/People - Active Projects.md
   - Organize by:
     * Family (always at top)
     * Project categories (Carbon Plant, EVOLVE, TTRO, etc.)

   - For each person, list:
     * Name with [[wiki link]]
     * Role/title
     * Projects involved
     * Organization

6. REPORT SUMMARY
   Provide user with:
   - Total people in active projects
   - New additions
   - Tier promotions/demotions
   - Removed/archived people
   - Recommended person note creation
```

### Tier Movement Signals

**Promotion signals (move up a tier):**

- Increasing interaction frequency
- Growing strategic importance
- Proven reliability and value
- Relationship deepening naturally
- Mutual investment increasing

**Demotion signals (move down a tier):**
- Decreasing interaction frequency
- Project completion/ending
- Reduced responsiveness
- Strategic importance declining
- Natural relationship drift
- One-sided effort

**Assessment cadence:**
- Tier 1-2: Review quarterly
- Tier 3: Review every 6 months
- Tier 4-5: Review annually or when reactivated

### Workflow 2: Assess Relationship Tier for Specific Person

**Trigger:** "How close am I to [person]?", "Assess my relationship with [person]"

**Process:**

```

   - Access to opportunities/networks

   - Tier 1: 3+ projects + weekly contact + critical impact
   - Tier 2: 1-2 projects + bi-weekly contact + high importance

6. PROVIDE RECOMMENDATION
   - Current tier classification

   - Relationship health assessment
   - Suggested actions (maintain, deepen, monitor)

**Tier Stability:**
- Measure: % of people remaining in same tier quarter-over-quarter
- Target: 70-80% stability (some movement is healthy)
- Alert: If >50% tier changes in single quarter (indicates assessment issues)

### Collaboration Metrics

**Strategic Partner Growth:**
- Measure: Number of Tier 2-3 people appearing in multiple projects
- Target: Increasing trend
- Success: Converting Tier 3 → Tier 2 based on multi-project collaboration

**Dependency Risk:**
- Measure: Number of critical projects with single-point dependencies
- Target: <20% of critical projects
- Alert: If >30% of projects depend on single person

**Relationship ROI:**
- Measure: Project success rate correlated with relationship tier
- Hypothesis: Projects with Tier 1-2 people should have higher success
- Track: Project health status by relationship tier of key contacts

---

## Best Practices

### Do's

✓ **Base tier assessment on data** - project count, interaction frequency, outcomes
✓ **Update regularly** - weekly reviews, after significant changes
✓ **Maintain proactively** - don't wait for Tier 1-2 people to reach out first
✓ **Document context** - person notes capture why relationships matter
✓ **Use Obsidian linking** - leverage graph view and backlinks
✓ **Track changes over time** - tier movements indicate relationship evolution
✓ **Balance investment** - More time on Tier 1-2, appropriate effort on Tier 3-4

### Don'ts

✗ **Don't over-tier people** - Most people should be Tier 3-4, reserve Tier 1-2 for truly strategic
✗ **Don't neglect data** - Feelings matter but data prevents bias
✗ **Don't create person notes for everyone** - Only Tier 1-3, maybe select Tier 4
✗ **Don't let Tier 1 relationships go stale** - These are critical, maintain actively
✗ **Don't ignore tier demotion signals** - Natural drift happens, adjust tiers accordingly
✗ **Don't make it personal** - Professional focus, objective assessment
✗ **Don't over-document** - Keep notes useful, not exhaustive

---

## Troubleshooting

**Problem:** People list getting out of date

**Solution:**
- Run "Update people list" workflow weekly
- Set calendar reminder
- Integrate with weekly review process

---

**Problem:** Unsure what tier someone should be

**Solution:**
- Run "Assess relationship tier" workflow
- Review tier framework criteria
- Check project involvement + interaction data
- When in doubt, tier conservatively (lower tier)
- Can always promote later

---

**Problem:** Too many Tier 1 relationships

**Solution:**
- Tier 1 should be ~5-10 people maximum
- Review each against strict criteria
- Be honest about "critical to life/work" test
- Demote to Tier 2 if not truly foundational
- Quality over quantity for core relationships

---

**Problem:** Single-point dependency on critical project

**Solution:**
- Identify who else in organization could be backup
- Request introduction to secondary contact
- Attend meetings with both contacts
- Document knowledge in project notes
- Develop parallel relationship intentionally

---

## Conclusion

This system helps you maintain a clear, data-driven view of your relationship network. By tracking who you work with, how close those relationships are, and monitoring health over time, you can:

- Invest appropriately in strategic relationships
- Catch issues before they become problems
- Discover emerging partnerships
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections that drive success

Remember: **Relationships are the foundation of all work.** This system just helps you manage them intentionally.

## Best Practices

### Do's

✓ **Base tier assessment on data** - project count, interaction frequency, outcomes
✓ **Update regularly** - weekly reviews, after significant changes
✓ **Maintain proactively** - don't wait for Tier 1-2 people to reach out first
✓ **Document context** - person notes capture why relationships matter
✓ **Use Obsidian linking** - leverage graph view and backlinks
✓ **Track changes over time** - tier movements indicate relationship evolution
✓ **Balance investment** - More time on Tier 1-2, appropriate effort on Tier 3-4

### Don'ts

✗ **Don't over-tier people** - Most people should be Tier 3-4, reserve Tier 1-2 for truly strategic
✗ **Don't neglect data** - Feelings matter but data prevents bias
✗ **Don't create person notes for everyone** - Only Tier 1-3, maybe select Tier 4
✗ **Don't let Tier 1 relationships go stale** - These are critical, maintain actively
✗ **Don't ignore tier demotion signals** - Natural drift happens, adjust tiers accordingly
✗ **Don't make it personal** - Professional focus, objective assessment
✗ **Don't over-document** - Keep notes useful, not exhaustive

---

## Troubleshooting

**Problem:** People list getting out of date

**Solution:**
- Run "Update people list" workflow weekly
- Set calendar reminder
- Integrate with weekly review process

---

**Problem:** Unsure what tier someone should be

**Solution:**
- Run "Assess relationship tier" workflow
- Review tier framework criteria
- Check project involvement + interaction data
- When in doubt, tier conservatively (lower tier)
- Can always promote later

---

**Problem:** Too many Tier 1 relationships

**Solution:**
- Tier 1 should be ~5-10 people maximum
- Review each against strict criteria
- Be honest about "critical to life/work" test
- Demote to Tier 2 if not truly foundational
- Quality over quantity for core relationships

---

**Problem:** Single-point dependency on critical project

**Solution:**
- Identify who else in organization could be backup
- Request introduction to secondary contact
- Attend meetings with both contacts
- Document knowledge in project notes
- Develop parallel relationship intentionally

---

## Conclusion

This system helps you maintain a clear, data-driven view of your relationship network. By tracking who you work with, how close those relationships are, and monitoring health over time, you can:

- Invest appropriately in strategic relationships
- Catch issues before they become problems
- Discover emerging partnerships
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections that drive success

Remember: **Relationships are the foundation of all work.** This system just helps you manage them intentionally.

✗ **Don't let Tier 1 relationships go stale** - These are critical, maintain actively
✗ **Don't ignore tier demotion signals** - Natural drift happens, adjust tiers accordingly
✗ **Don't make it personal** - Professional focus, objective assessment
✗ **Don't over-document** - Keep notes useful, not exhaustive

---

## Troubleshooting

**Problem:** People list getting out of date

**Solution:**
- Run "Update people list" workflow weekly
- Set calendar reminder
- Integrate with weekly review process

---

**Problem:** Unsure what tier someone should be

**Solution:**
- Run "Assess relationship tier" workflow
- Review tier framework criteria
- Check project involvement + interaction data
- When in doubt, tier conservatively (lower tier)
- Can always promote later

---

**Problem:** Too many Tier 1 relationships

**Solution:**
- Tier 1 should be ~5-10 people maximum
- Review each against strict criteria
- Be honest about "critical to life/work" test
- Demote to Tier 2 if not truly foundational
- Quality over quantity for core relationships

---

**Problem:** Single-point dependency on critical project

**Solution:**
- Identify who else in organization could be backup
- Request introduction to secondary contact
- Attend meetings with both contacts
- Document knowledge in project notes
- Develop parallel relationship intentionally

---

## Conclusion

This system helps you maintain a clear, data-driven view of your relationship network. By tracking who you work with, how close those relationships are, and monitoring health over time, you can:

- Invest appropriately in strategic relationships
- Catch issues before they become problems
- Discover emerging partnerships
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections that drive success

Remember: **Relationships are the foundation of all work.** This system just helps you manage them intentionally.

1. [System Overview](#system-overview)
2. [Vault Structure](#vault-structure)

## System Overview

### Philosophy

This system treats **relationships as the foundation of all work**. Projects succeed or fail based on the people involved. By tracking relationship closeness, collaboration patterns, and interaction health, we can:

- Identify strategic partners worth investing in
- Catch relationship issues before they become project blockers
- Discover emerging collaborators who deserve more attention
- Prevent single-point dependencies
- Maintain strong connections with core relationships

### Core Capabilities

1. **People List Management** - Maintain accurate, categorized lists of who you work with
2. **Relationship Tier Assessment** - Objectively evaluate closeness/importance (1-5 scale)
3. **Collaboration Analysis** - Map people to projects, find patterns, identify risks
4. **Person Note Creation** - Individual pages for key relationships with context
5. **Health Monitoring** - Track interaction frequency, flag stale relationships
6. **Strategic Planning** - Identify who to invest in, who to maintain, who to archive

---

## Vault Structure

### Base Path
```
/Users/irautenbach/Documents/Obsidian/Personal/
```

### Key Directories

**Projects & Efforts:**
```
3 Efforts/ON/           # Active projects (PT*.md, OPT*.md files)
3 Efforts/Ongoing/      # Ongoing projects
3 Efforts Notes/        # Project support notes and resources
```

**Knowledge Base:**
```
Atlas Dots/             # Atomic notes (people, concepts, tools)

```

**Reference & History:**
```
Companies/              # Company/organization notes

0 INBOX/                # Unsorted incoming notes
```

### File Naming Conventions

- `OPT [Opportunity Name].md` - Business opportunities

**Person files:**

**List files:**

---

## Relationship Tier Framework

### 5-Tier System

People are categorized by their **closeness** and **importance** to your life and work. Tiers should be based on objective data, not just feelings.

---

### Tier 1: Core (Pivotal to Life & Work)

**Definition:** These people are foundational. Your work and life would be significantly different without them.

**Characteristics:**
- Daily or weekly interaction
- Critical to multiple major projects
- Deep trust and long-term relationship (typically 1+ years)
- Significant impact on business/personal trajectory
- Losing this relationship would require major adjustment
- High emotional and professional investment

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 3+ active projects
- Contact every 1-14 days
- Projects with them have high success rate
- Recurring collaboration over 12+ months
- Decision-making influence

**Maintenance:**
- Proactive contact every 1-2 weeks minimum
- Regular check-ins beyond project needs
- Invest in relationship deepening
- Priority response time
- Share strategic thinking

**Current examples:**

- **Strategic partners:** Kirsty Chadwick (TTRO - multiple opportunities), Ron Dahlgren (Connected IQ - technical foundation), Michael Cosgrave (Glenart - strategic business)

**Typical roles:**
- Life partner, immediate family
- Co-founders, business partners
- Long-term strategic collaborators
- Key advisors with proven track record

---

### Tier 2: Strategic Partners (High Importance)

**Definition:** Highly important to current success, key to 1-2 major initiatives.

**Characteristics:**
- Regular interaction (weekly to bi-weekly)
- Key to 1-2 major projects (not just supporting role)
- Proven track record of delivery
- Strategic value to business growth
- Strong professional relationship
- Would impact success if relationship ended

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1-2 active projects in key roles
- Contact every 1-4 weeks
- Reliable delivery and communication
- Projects with them generally succeed
- Mutual value exchange

**Maintenance:**
- Contact every 2-4 weeks
- Regular project check-ins
- Occasional non-project relationship building
- Good response priority
- Share relevant opportunities

**Current examples:**
- Yanis Hammick (Carbon Plant - product lead)
- David Halley (Gfinity/Connected IQ - recurring partner)
- Adam Shore (Liverpool University - institutional partnership)
- Miles Ashworth (IoM - ongoing client projects)

**Typical roles:**
- Key clients with ongoing work
- Primary contacts at strategic organizations
- Reliable technical leads
- Important institutional partners

---

### Tier 3: Active Collaborators (Regular Contact)

**Definition:** Active working relationships with specific scope and regular interaction.

**Characteristics:**
- Project-based interaction (during active phases)
- Specific expertise or defined role
- Reliable within their scope
- Professional relationship established
- Could become strategic over time
- Relationship tied to project lifecycle

**Data signals:**
- Appears in 1 active project
- Contact every 1-8 weeks (project-dependent)
- Delivers on defined scope
- Professional but not deeply personal
- Clear role and boundaries

**Maintenance:**
- Contact based on project needs
- Professional communication
- Responsive to their needs
- Evaluate for tier promotion if multi-project collaboration emerges

**Typical roles:**

- Professional service providers
- Active opportunity contacts

---

### Tier 4: Occasional/Emerging (New or Infrequent)

**Definition:** Early-stage relationships or infrequent collaborators with potential.

**Characteristics:**
- New relationship (< 6 months)
- Infrequent interaction
- Exploratory or single-project
- Potential for growth unclear
- Still establishing trust and value
- Networking or opportunistic

**Data signals:**
- Recently met or minimal project involvement
- Contact every 1-3 months (or sporadic)
- Single meeting/project or exploratory discussions
- Potential value not yet proven
- Relationship still being evaluated

**Maintenance:**
- Opportunistic contact
- Responsive when they reach out
- Evaluate after 3-6 months
- Low-cost relationship investment
- Monitor for tier promotion signals

**Current examples:**

- Brendan Kenny (Isle of Man)

**Typical roles:**
- New business contacts
- Conference/event connections
- Referral introductions
- Exploratory opportunity contacts
- Network connections

---

### Tier 5: Passive (Past or Minimal Contact)

**Definition:** Historical relationships, past collaborators, or inactive connections.

**Characteristics:**
- No current active projects
- Minimal or no interaction (3+ months)
- Completed/ended project history
- Relationship may reactivate in future
- Low current relevance
- Archived but not forgotten

**Data signals:**
- No appearance in active projects
- Last contact > 90 days
- Project completion or opportunity passed
- No active mutual value exchange
- Relationship on hold

**Maintenance:**
- Passive monitoring only
- Annual check-in (optional)
- Responsive if they reach out
- Consider archiving person note
- Re-tier if relationship reactivates

**Current examples:**
- Past project collaborators
- Declined opportunities
- Moved on to other roles
- Archived business contacts

**Typical roles:**
- Former colleagues
- Past clients
- Completed project teams
- Stale networking contacts

---

### Tier Movement Signals

**Promotion signals (move up a tier):**
- Appearing in additional projects
- Increasing interaction frequency
- Growing strategic importance
- Proven reliability and value
- Relationship deepening naturally
- Mutual investment increasing

**Demotion signals (move down a tier):**
- Decreasing interaction frequency
- Project completion/ending
- Reduced responsiveness
- Strategic importance declining
- Natural relationship drift
- One-sided effort

**Assessment cadence:**
- Tier 1-2: Review quarterly
- Tier 3: Review every 6 months
- Tier 4-5: Review annually or when reactivated

   - 3+ projects + key roles = Tier 1-2 candidate

   - Single project = Tier 3-4
   - Mentioned but no active role = Tier 4-5

4. UPDATE MASTER LIST

   Provide user with:

  - JavaScript/TypeScript: bun (NOT npm, yarn, or pnpm)
  - Python (if needed): uv (NOT pip)

---

## General Instructions

1. **Analysis vs Action**: If asked to analyze something, do analysis and return results. Don't change things unless explicitly asked.

2. **Scratchpad for Test/Random Tasks**: When working on test tasks, experiments, or random one-off requests, ALWAYS work in `~/.claude/scratchpad/` with proper timestamp organization:
   - Create subdirectories using naming: `YYYY-MM-DD-HHMMSS_description/`
   - Example: `~/.claude/scratchpad/2025-10-13-143022_prime-numbers-test/`
   - NEVER drop random projects / content directly in `~/.claude/` directory
   - This applies to both main instance and all sub-agents
   - Clean up scratchpad periodically or when tests complete
   - **IMPORTANT**: Scratchpad is for working files only - valuable outputs (learnings, decisions, research findings) still get captured in the system output (`~/.claude/history/`) via hooks

3. **Hooks**: Configured in `~/.claude/settings.json`

4. **Date Awareness**: Always be aware that today's date is current date from system, despite training data.

---

## Response Format

**Recommended format for responses:**

```
📅 [Use actual current date from system: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS]
📋 SUMMARY: Brief overview of request and accomplishment
🔍 ANALYSIS: Key findings and context
⚡ ACTIONS: Steps taken with tools used
✅ RESULTS: Outcomes and changes made - SHOW ACTUAL OUTPUT CONTENT
📊 STATUS: Current state after completion
➡️ NEXT: Recommended follow-up actions
🎯 COMPLETED: Completed [task description in 6 words]
```

---

## Key Contacts

- writer: [your-voice-id]

---

## 🚨 SECURITY SECTION CRITICAL 🚨

### Repository Safety

- **NEVER Post sensitive data to public repos**
- **NEVER COMMIT FROM THE WRONG DIRECTORY** - Always verify which repository
- **CHECK THE REMOTE** - Run `git remote -v` BEFORE committing
- **`~/.claude/` MAY CONTAIN SENSITIVE PRIVATE DATA** - Be careful with public repos
- **CHECK THREE TIMES** before git add/commit from any directory
- **ALWAYS COMMIT PROJECT FILES FROM THEIR OWN DIRECTORIES**
- Before public repo commits, ensure NO sensitive content (credentials, keys, passwords, personal data)
- If worried about sensitive content, review carefully before committing

Be **EXTREMELY CAUTIOUS** when working with:
- Cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure)
- DNS and domain management (Cloudflare, etc.)
- Any core production-supporting services

Always verify operations before significantly modifying or deleting infrastructure. For GitHub, ensure save/restore points exist.
